# Microreactors.org: How microreactors work, in interactive 3D

Source: https://microreactors.org/  Updated: 2026-11-02

A representative, vendor-neutral educational model. Values are typical of a 10 MWe class pool-type sodium-cooled microreactor and of a data center of about 8 MW. They do not describe a specific product.

## What is a microreactor?

### The short answer

A microreactor is a small nuclear power plant. It makes up to about 20 megawatts of electricity, or about 50 megawatts of heat. A factory builds the reactor as one module. A truck, a train, or a ship delivers it to the site.

The size changes how nuclear power gets built. A large plant takes a decade and a city-sized construction site. A microreactor arrives nearly complete, and the site work takes months. The plant can then sit next to the load it serves: a data center, a mine, a remote town, a military base, or a factory that needs heat.

Most designs run for years without refueling. Many use high-assay low-enriched uranium, called HALEU, which holds between 5 and 20 percent uranium-235. The small core and the long fuel life let one or two operators oversee the plant, with a remote center watching too.

### How the plant in the 3D model works

The model shows a representative sodium-cooled, pool-type microreactor of about 10 megawatts electric and 30 megawatts thermal. Sixty-one hexagonal fuel assemblies sit in a compact core about 1.2 meters across. A reflector ring around the core bounces neutrons back in, so a small core can sustain the chain reaction.

Twelve control drums sit inside the reflector. Each drum has a neutron-absorbing face. Turned toward the core, the drum lowers power. Turned away, it raises power. Three shutdown rods hang above the core on electromagnets. If the magnets lose power, the rods drop by gravity and stop the reaction in under two seconds.

Liquid sodium fills the reactor vessel. It enters the core at about 400 °C and leaves at about 550 °C. Sodium boils at 883 °C, so the vessel runs at near atmospheric pressure. Two electromagnetic pumps move the sodium with magnetic fields and no moving parts. If they stop, natural circulation keeps the sodium moving.

Two intermediate heat exchangers pass the heat to a clean intermediate loop. That loop leaves the reactor vault and feeds the power conversion unit. A supercritical carbon dioxide turbine spins a generator and makes about 10 megawatts. Fans blow air across finned tubes to reject the waste heat. The plant uses no cooling water.

The whole reactor module ships on one steel skid. A heavy-haul trailer brings it from the factory. A bridge crane lifts it into a concrete shield silo inside the reactor building. The silo gives radiation shielding, seismic protection, and a final barrier for sodium.

### How it stays safe

The design relies on physics rather than on pumps, valves, or operators. The sodium pool is large, so it absorbs heat slowly. After shutdown, the fuel still makes a few percent of full power. Air ducts around the guard vessel let natural convection carry that heat up a chimney. This system has no pumps and no power supply, and it is always on.

A second steel vessel, the guard vessel, surrounds the reactor vessel with a small argon-filled gap. If the inner vessel leaks, the guard vessel catches the sodium and keeps the core covered. Thick concrete and borated steel around the vessel absorb neutrons and gamma rays, so workers can approach the building while the reactor runs.

Sodium reacts with water and air, so it stays inside sealed steel systems under an argon cover gas. The intermediate loop keeps radioactive sodium inside the reactor vault. Only clean fluid reaches the turbine hall.

### How it powers a data center

A short 69 kV line on steel poles carries the plant output to a campus substation. Two transformers step the voltage down to 13.8 kV and feed the data hall through an underground duct bank. The hall holds about 320 racks and draws about 8 megawatts of IT load, plus cooling and losses.

The reactor runs flat out all the time. Battery containers absorb or supply the difference as the load moves, and they can black-start the campus. UPS units ride through short dips. Two standby diesel generators cover the hall if the reactor or the line is out. With the reactor as prime power, they run only for tests.

Rooftop dry coolers reject the heat the servers make. Like the reactor, the data center uses no cooling water.

### Other kinds of microreactors

Not every microreactor uses liquid sodium in a pool. The demonstration park down the road shows three other designs at a basic level. A heat-pipe reactor has no pumps and no coolant loop at all. Sealed sodium heat pipes carry heat out of a solid core block. A gas-cooled reactor circulates helium through TRISO fuel, and this one stores heat in molten salt tanks like a thermal battery. A molten-salt reactor dissolves the fuel in the coolant itself and drains it to a safe tank if power fails.

Each design trades one set of engineering problems for another. The reactor types page compares them side by side.

### About this model

The 3D plant is a representative design for education. It does not describe a specific company or product. The values are typical of a 10 MWe class pool-type sodium-cooled microreactor and of a data center of about 8 MW. Regulators review every real design before it can operate, and real plants will differ in detail.

You can cut the model open, explode it, search every part, run the start-up sequence, change the physics live, and walk the site on foot. The written guide lists every labeled component with its role and typical specifications.

### The 60-second tour, in words

1. What is a microreactor?. A nuclear power plant small enough to build in a factory and deliver on a truck.
2. Ten megawatts of electricity. That is enough for about 8,000 homes, or for one data hall.
3. One module, one truck. The reactor sits in a steel vessel inside a concrete silo. The whole module arrives on one truck.
4. Fuel pins and control drums. Uranium fuel pins heat up. Twelve rotating drums set the power level.
5. Liquid sodium carries the heat. Sodium moves heat out of the core. It stays liquid without pressure.
6. Heat becomes electricity. A turbine turns the heat into power. Fans reject the waste heat, so the plant needs no cooling water.
7. A data center next door. A short line carries the power to the data hall. Batteries and generators keep the servers up.
8. It shuts itself down. Rods drop by gravity and stop the reaction. Air alone carries away the leftover heat.
9. Heat pipes, helium, and molten salt. Other microreactors use different coolants. Three of them stand in the park down the road.
10. Now it is yours. Cut it open. Run the physics. Walk the site.

### Frequently asked questions

Q: What is a microreactor?
A: A microreactor is a small nuclear reactor that makes up to about 20 megawatts of electricity. A factory builds it as one module, and a truck can deliver it. Most designs run for years without refueling and use passive safety systems.

Q: How much power does a microreactor make?
A: Between about 1 and 20 megawatts of electricity. The plant in this model makes 10 megawatts electric from 30 megawatts of heat. That is enough for about 8,000 homes, or for one data hall of about 8 megawatts of IT load.

Q: How big is a microreactor?
A: The reactor vessel in the model is about 5.5 meters tall and 2.4 meters across. The module ships on one truck. The reactor building is about 18 by 12 meters, and the whole fenced site covers a few acres.

Q: What fuel does a microreactor use?
A: Most designs use high-assay low-enriched uranium, or HALEU, with less than 20 percent uranium-235. The sodium-cooled plant uses metal or oxide fuel pins in steel cladding. The gas-cooled and heat-pipe designs use TRISO particles, which wear ceramic coatings that hold fission products to above 1,600 °C.

Q: How often does a microreactor refuel?
A: The sodium-cooled model swaps its whole core every 5 to 10 years. The heat-pipe module runs about 8 years, then the whole module is replaced. The gas-cooled design in the park runs about 20 years on one core.

Q: Why use liquid sodium as a coolant?
A: Sodium conducts heat very well and stays liquid from 98 °C to 883 °C. The reactor can run hot at near atmospheric pressure, with no thick pressure vessel. Sodium reacts with water and air, so it stays in sealed steel systems under argon, and an intermediate loop keeps it out of the turbine hall.

Q: How is a microreactor controlled?
A: Rotating control drums in the reflector set the power. Each drum has a neutron-absorbing face. Turned toward the core, it lowers power; turned away, it raises power. The control system turns the drums on its own, and operators oversee it.

Q: What happens if the power fails?
A: The shutdown rods hang on electromagnets. When power is lost, they drop by gravity and stop the chain reaction in under two seconds. The sodium keeps moving by natural circulation. Air ducts around the vessel carry away the decay heat with no pumps and no power.

Q: Does a microreactor need cooling water?
A: No. The plant in the model rejects its waste heat with fans and finned tubes. The data center next door uses rooftop dry coolers. Neither uses cooling water.

Q: How does a microreactor power a data center?
A: A short 69 kV line carries the output to a campus substation. Transformers step it down to 13.8 kV for the hall. Batteries follow the load, UPS units ride through dips, and standby generators cover outages. The reactor runs flat out as prime power.

Q: What other kinds of microreactors exist?
A: Heat-pipe reactors move heat with sealed sodium pipes and have no pumps. Gas-cooled reactors circulate helium through TRISO fuel, often with molten salt heat storage. Molten-salt reactors dissolve the fuel in the coolant. The demonstration park in the model shows one of each.

Q: How many people run a microreactor?
A: The model assumes two operators and one security officer on shift, with a remote monitoring center. The reactor controls itself, so the control room is small.

Q: Is this 3D model a real product?
A: No. It is a representative, vendor-neutral design for education. The numbers are typical ranges for a 10 MWe class sodium-cooled microreactor and an 8 MW data center. Real plants will differ in detail, and regulators review each design before it operates.

## Four kinds of microreactor, side by side

The four plants in the 3D model use four different ways to move heat out of a small core. Each choice sets the pressure, the temperature, the fuel form, and the kind of safety case the design can make. The table lists the values the model uses. They are typical of each class, not a specific product.

| Feature | Sodium pool (main plant) | Heat pipe | Gas-cooled | Molten salt |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Coolant | Liquid sodium in a pool | Sodium inside sealed heat pipes | Helium gas | Fluoride salt that also carries the fuel |
| Fuel | HALEU metal or oxide pins in steel cladding | TRISO compacts in a solid block | TRISO particles | Uranium dissolved in the salt |
| Thermal power | ≈ 30 MWt | ≈ 15 MWt | ≈ 15 MWt | ≈ 30 MWt |
| Electric output | ≈ 10 MWe | ≈ 5 MWe | ≈ 5 MWe | ≈ 10 MWe |
| Pressure | Near atmospheric | Near atmospheric | ≈ 7 MPa | Near atmospheric |
| Core outlet temperature | ≈ 550 °C | ≈ 650 °C | ≈ 630 °C | ≈ 650 °C |
| Power cycle | Supercritical CO₂ Brayton | Open-air Brayton | Steam Rankine with salt storage | Steam Rankine |
| Refueling | Whole-core swap every 5 to 10 years | Swap the module after about 8 years | About 20 years on one core | Fuel salt adjusted on line |
| Moving parts in the core loop | Electromagnetic pumps, no impellers | None | One helium circulator | One fuel-salt pump |
| Signature safety feature | Natural-draft air cooling of the vessel | Heat leaves by conduction, no coolant to lose | Fuel coatings hold fission products above 1,600 °C | Freeze plug drains the fuel to a safe tank |
| Where in the model | Main plant, powering the data center | Park plot A, canister open | Park plot B, with two salt tanks | Park plot C, reactor cell |

The sodium pool and the molten-salt designs run hot at low pressure, so they avoid a thick pressure vessel. The gas-cooled design accepts high pressure in return for an inert coolant that cannot boil. The heat-pipe design removes pumps and valves from the core entirely, at the cost of lower power per module.
All four reject their waste heat to air. None of them needs cooling water.

## Reactor core: fuel, reflector, control drums, shutdown rods

Page: https://microreactors.org/guide/reactor-core/

The core is where fission happens. It is small, about 1.2 meters across and 1 meter tall, and it makes about 30 megawatts of heat. These parts hold the fuel, reflect neutrons back in, set the power, and stop the reaction when needed.

### Reactor core

The core is the compact region where fission takes place. Fuel assemblies sit in a tight hexagonal lattice, and the reflector surrounds them.

- Thermal power: ≈ 30 MWt
- Active height: ≈ 1.0 m
- Diameter: ≈ 1.2 m
- Refueling: Whole-core swap every 5–10 years

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#core

### Fuel assemblies

Each assembly is a hexagonal steel duct that holds a bundle of fuel pins. Sodium flows upward through the duct and carries the heat away.

- Count: 61
- Duct material: HT-9 ferritic steel
- Lattice pitch: ≈ 135 mm
- Pins per assembly: 91, wire-wrapped

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#assemblies

### Fuel pins

Fuel pins are sealed steel tubes filled with uranium fuel pellets. A wire wrapped around each pin keeps the pins apart and lets sodium flow between them.

- Fuel form: U-Zr metal or UO₂, HALEU (< 20% U-235)
- Cladding: HT-9 steel
- Pin diameter: ≈ 9 mm
- Peak cladding temp.: ≈ 650 °C

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#pins

### Neutron reflector

The reflector ring surrounds the core and bounces escaping neutrons back in. It lets a small core sustain a chain reaction with less fuel.

- Material: Beryllium oxide or graphite in steel cans
- Radial thickness: ≈ 280 mm
- Height: ≈ 1.1 m
- Also houses: 12 control drums

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#reflector

### Control drums

Control drums are rotating cylinders inside the reflector. One face is a neutron absorber: turned toward the core it lowers power, turned away it raises power.

- Count: 12
- Absorber: Boron carbide (B₄C) sector, 120°
- Diameter: ≈ 220 mm
- Drive: Stepper motor, 0–180° rotation

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#drums

### Shutdown rods

Shutdown rods drop into the core to stop the chain reaction. Gravity inserts them when the holding magnets lose power, so the system needs no operator action.

- Count: 3
- Absorber: Boron carbide (B₄C)
- Insertion time: < 2 s
- Hold: Electromagnetic latch, fail-safe

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#rods

## Sodium primary system: vessel, pool, pumps, heat exchangers

Page: https://microreactors.org/guide/sodium-primary-system/

The primary system holds the core in a pool of liquid sodium at near atmospheric pressure. Pumps with no moving parts drive the sodium, heat exchangers hand the heat to a clean loop, and a second vessel catches any leak.

### Reactor vessel

The reactor vessel is a stainless-steel tank that holds the core and the sodium pool. It operates near atmospheric pressure because sodium boils at 883 °C, far above operating temperature.

- Material: 316H stainless steel
- Height: ≈ 5.5 m
- Diameter: ≈ 2.4 m
- Design pressure: Near atmospheric

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#vessel

### Guard vessel

A second steel vessel surrounds the reactor vessel with a small gap. If the inner vessel leaks, the guard vessel catches the sodium and keeps the core covered.

- Gap: ≈ 150 mm, argon filled
- Material: Stainless steel
- Leak detection: Gap sensors and level probes
- Function: Second barrier for sodium

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#guard

### Sodium coolant pool

Liquid sodium fills the vessel and carries heat from the core to the heat exchangers. It conducts heat very well and stays liquid from 98 °C to 883 °C.

- Core inlet: ≈ 400 °C
- Core outlet: ≈ 550 °C
- Inventory: ≈ 20 tonnes
- Cover gas: Argon at ~1 atm

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#sodium

### Electromagnetic pumps

EM pumps drive sodium with magnetic fields instead of impellers. They have no moving parts, no seals, and nothing to wear out.

- Count: 2
- Type: Annular linear induction
- Flow: ≈ 150 kg/s each
- Backup: Natural circulation

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#pumps

### Intermediate heat exchangers

The IHX moves heat from the radioactive primary sodium to a clean intermediate loop. Thousands of thin tubes give the two fluids a large contact area without mixing.

- Count: 2
- Type: Shell-and-tube, counter-flow
- Duty: ≈ 15 MWt each
- Secondary fluid: Sodium or molten salt

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#ihx

### Reactor head & drives

The head closes the vessel and carries every penetration. Rod drives, instrument lines, and pipe nozzles pass through it, and a rotating plug gives access for refueling.

- Deck thickness: ≈ 300 mm steel
- Rotating plug: ≈ 1.8 m diameter
- Penetrations: Rod drives, IHX nozzles, instruments
- Shield plug: Borated steel and concrete below deck

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#head

## Safety and shielding: decay heat removal, shielding, instruments

Page: https://microreactors.org/guide/safety-and-shielding/

Safety in this design comes from physics. Decay heat leaves by natural air flow with no pumps. Thick shielding lets workers approach the building. Sensors report on the core in real time, and the control system acts on them.

### Decay heat removal

After shutdown the fuel still produces a few percent of full power. Air ducts around the guard vessel let natural convection carry that heat to a chimney with no pumps and no power.

- Type: Reactor vessel auxiliary cooling (RVACS)
- Capacity: ≈ 1 MWt
- Driving force: Natural draft
- Availability: Always on, passive

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#dhr

### Radiation shielding

Thick concrete and steel around the vessel absorb neutrons and gamma rays. Workers can approach the building while the reactor operates.

- Material: Reinforced concrete and borated steel
- Radial thickness: ≈ 1.4 m
- Top shield: Rotating shield plug
- Design goal: Public dose limits met at site boundary

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#shield

### Instrumentation

Neutron detectors, thermocouples, and sodium level sensors report on the core in real time. The control system uses these readings to adjust the drums automatically.

- Neutron detectors: 4 ex-core fission chambers
- Temperature: ≈ 200 thermocouples
- Leak detection: Guard-vessel gap sensors
- Operation: Autonomous with remote monitoring

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#instruments

## Power conversion: intermediate loop, turbine, dry cooling

Page: https://microreactors.org/guide/power-conversion/

Heat leaves the reactor vault in a clean intermediate loop. A supercritical carbon dioxide turbine turns it into about 10 megawatts of electricity. Fans reject the waste heat, so the plant needs no cooling water.

### Intermediate loop piping

Insulated pipes carry the clean intermediate fluid from the IHX to the power conversion unit and back. The loop keeps radioactive sodium inside the reactor vault.

- Pipes: 2 hot legs, 2 cold legs
- Hot leg: ≈ 520 °C
- Cold leg: ≈ 370 °C
- Insulation: Mineral wool with steel jacket

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#loop

### Power conversion unit

The PCU turns heat into electricity. Hot intermediate fluid heats a working gas that spins a turbine and a generator.

- Cycle: Supercritical CO₂ Brayton
- Net output: ≈ 10 MWe
- Efficiency: ≈ 35–40%
- Footprint: One truck-transportable skid

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#pcu

### Air-cooled heat rejection

Fans blow air across finned tubes to reject the waste heat of the power cycle. Dry cooling means the plant needs no cooling water.

- Type: Forced-draft dry cooler
- Heat rejected: ≈ 20 MWt
- Fans: 6 × 3 m diameter
- Water use: None

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#cooler

## Site and buildings: reactor building, crane, truck, control room, casks

Page: https://microreactors.org/guide/site-and-buildings/

The reactor module arrives on one truck and sets into a concrete silo inside a steel building. A small control building, a used fuel cask pad, and a bridge crane complete the site.

### Reactor building

A steel building encloses the reactor module and the power unit. Inside it, a concrete shield silo holds the module, gives seismic protection, and forms a final barrier for sodium.

- Footprint: ≈ 18 × 12 m
- Shield silo: ≈ 1.4 m reinforced concrete
- Structure: Steel frame, insulated panels
- Seismic: Module on isolated base

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#building

### Bridge crane

An overhead bridge crane runs the length of the building. It lifts the reactor head, the shield plug, and the spent core cask during refueling.

- Capacity: ≈ 40 t
- Span: ≈ 12 m
- Hoist: Electric wire-rope, two speeds
- Use: Refueling and major maintenance

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#crane

### Module delivery truck

A heavy-haul trailer brings a complete reactor module from the factory. The crane lifts the skid off the trailer and sets it in the silo.

- Load: One module on its skid, ≈ 80 t
- Trailer: Lowboy, multi-axle
- Permits: Standard oversize-load route
- Factory to site: Days, not months

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#truck

### Control & operations building

Operators monitor the plant from this building. The reactor runs on its own, and the control system needs only oversight, so the room is small.

- Staff on shift: 2 operators, 1 security
- Monitoring: Local control room plus remote center
- Also inside: Offices, instrument shop, break room
- Footprint: ≈ 14 × 6 m, two floors

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#control

### Used fuel cask pad

After a core swap, the used core cools in a steel and concrete cask on this pad. The casks are passive, need no power, and ship off site later.

- Casks: 4 positions
- Shielding: Steel canister in a concrete overpack
- Cooling: Passive air, no power
- Dose at fence: Below public limits

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#casks

### Transport skid

The reactor module ships from the factory on a steel skid. The skid sets the module in the shield silo and acts as its seismic base.

- Fits: Standard heavy-haul trailer
- Mass: ≈ 80 t with module
- Transport: Truck or rail
- Install time: Weeks, not years

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#skid

## Grid connection: transmission line, substation, switchyard

Page: https://microreactors.org/guide/grid-connection/

A short line carries the output to the campus substation and a second circuit ties the plant to the regional grid. Transformers and switchgear protect the plant and let operators isolate it.

### Transmission line

A short line carries the plant output to the campus substation. A second circuit on lattice towers ties the plant to the regional grid.

- Voltage: 69 kV, three phase
- Campus line: ≈ 30 m on steel monopoles
- Grid tie: Lattice towers to the regional network
- Capacity: ≈ 12 MW, far above plant output

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#txline

### Campus substation

The campus substation steps the voltage down for the data center. Two transformers share the load so one can rest during maintenance.

- Transformers: 2 × 8 MVA, 69 kV to 13.8 kV
- Redundancy: N+1, either unit carries the hall
- Protection: Breakers and relays in the switch house
- Feed to hall: Underground duct bank

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#dcsub

### Switchyard & transformer

The generator output steps up through a transformer to the local grid voltage. Switchgear cabinets protect the plant and let operators isolate it from the grid.

- Transformer: ≈ 12 MVA, 13.8 kV to 69 kV
- Switchgear: Metal-clad, 3 cabinets
- Connection: Single feeder to local grid or microgrid
- Islanding: Can run isolated with a load bank

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#switchyard

## The data center: hall, racks, UPS, batteries, generators, cooling

Page: https://microreactors.org/guide/data-center/

The data hall is the load. It holds about 320 racks and draws about 8 megawatts. Batteries follow the load, UPS units ride through dips, standby generators cover outages, and rooftop coolers reject the heat.

### Data hall

The data hall holds the servers that use the reactor output. One microreactor carries roughly 8 MW of IT load plus cooling and losses.

- Footprint: ≈ 48 × 22 m
- IT load: ≈ 8 MW
- Racks: 320 at ≈ 25 kW each
- Uptime target: Tier III, concurrently maintainable

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#dchall

### Server racks

Servers sit in rows of racks with hot-aisle containment. Cold air enters the front of each rack and hot air leaves into a sealed aisle.

- Rows: 8 rows × 40 racks
- Rack power: ≈ 25 kW, liquid-ready
- Containment: Hot aisle, doors at each end
- Distribution: Overhead busway, A and B feeds

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#racks

### UPS & electrical room

The electrical room receives the feed from the substation and conditions it. UPS units ride through short dips while the generators start.

- UPS: 2 × 5 MW, N+1
- Ride-through: ≈ 5 minutes at full load
- Switchgear: 13.8 kV to 480 V
- Distribution: PDUs feed the overhead busway

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#ups

### Battery storage

Battery containers smooth the load the reactor sees. The reactor runs flat out, and the batteries absorb or supply the difference.

- Capacity: ≈ 10 MWh in 3 containers
- Power: ≈ 5 MW
- Chemistry: Lithium iron phosphate
- Role: Load following and black start

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#bess

### Backup generators

Standby generators cover the hall if the reactor or the line is out. With the reactor as prime power, they run only for tests.

- Units: 2 × 3 MW
- Fuel: Diesel, 24 hours on site
- Start time: < 10 s to full load
- Duty: Standby, monthly test

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#gens

### Cooling plant

Rooftop coolers reject the heat the servers make. Fans pull air across coils, and the chilled loop returns to the hall.

- Heat rejected: ≈ 9 MW
- Units: 6 rooftop dry coolers
- Loop: Warm water, 30 °C supply
- Water use: None, dry cooling

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#dccool

## Heat-pipe microreactor: how it works

Page: https://microreactors.org/guide/heat-pipe-microreactor/

The heat-pipe reactor in the park has no pumps and no coolant loop. Sealed sodium heat pipes carry heat out of a solid core block to an air turbine. The whole reactor ships inside one canister.

### Heat-pipe reactor module

This sister plant has no pumps and no liquid coolant loop. The whole reactor ships inside one steel canister on a truck, and the lid is off here so you can see inside.

- Electric output: ≈ 5 MWe
- Thermal power: ≈ 15 MWt
- Canister: ≈ 3 m dia × 10 m
- Core life: ≈ 8 years, then swap the module

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#hp_canister

### Monolith core

The core is one solid block with fuel channels and heat-pipe channels drilled through it. Heat moves from the fuel into the block, then into the pipes. Nothing flows inside the core.

- Fuel: TRISO particles in compacts
- Block: Graphite or steel monolith
- Diameter: ≈ 1.6 m
- Length: ≈ 2.4 m

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#hp_core

### Sodium heat pipes

Each pipe is a sealed tube with a little sodium inside. Sodium boils at the hot end, the vapor flows to the cold end, condenses, and a wick pulls the liquid back. No pump, no valve, no power.

- Count: ≈ 100 to 200
- Working fluid: Sodium, a few hundred grams per pipe
- Operating temperature: ≈ 650 °C
- Heat per pipe: ≈ 100 kW

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#hp_pipes

### Control drums

Drums in the reflector turn to bring an absorber face toward or away from the core. They are the same idea as the drums in the sodium plant.

- Count: 12
- Absorber: Boron carbide
- Drive: Electric motor, fail-safe spring

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#hp_drums

### Heat-pipe heat exchanger

The cold ends of the heat pipes pass through this block. Air or carbon dioxide flows around them, picks up the heat, and goes to the turbine.

- Working gas: Air or supercritical CO₂
- Gas outlet temperature: ≈ 600 °C
- Size: ≈ 2 × 2 × 1.5 m

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#hp_hx

### Open-air Brayton skid

A gas turbine and generator sit on one skid outside the canister. Air comes in through the filter house, goes through the heat exchanger, spins the turbine, and leaves through the stack.

- Cycle: Open-air Brayton
- Electric output: ≈ 5 MWe
- Cooling water: None
- Footprint: ≈ 12 × 4 m

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#hp_pcu

## Gas-cooled microreactor with salt storage: how it works

Page: https://microreactors.org/guide/gas-cooled-microreactor/

The gas-cooled reactor in the park circulates helium through TRISO fuel. Hot helium heats molten salt, and two tanks store the salt like a thermal battery, so the turbine can follow the data center while the reactor runs flat out.

### Helium pressure vessel

This plant cools its core with helium gas under pressure. Helium does not react with anything and cannot boil. The vessel is a tall steel cylinder with the core in the middle.

- Coolant: Helium at ≈ 7 MPa
- Core outlet: ≈ 630 °C
- Thermal power: ≈ 15 MWt
- Core life: ≈ 20 years

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#ht_vessel

### TRISO fuel

Each fuel kernel is smaller than a poppy seed and wears four ceramic coatings. The coatings hold in fission products to well above 1,600 °C. The display case shows one particle cut open at large scale.

- Kernel: Uranium oxycarbide, ≈ 0.5 mm
- Coatings: Buffer, PyC, SiC, PyC
- Particle size: ≈ 1 mm
- Particles per reactor: Billions

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#ht_fuel

### Helium circulator

A motor-driven blower on top of the vessel pushes helium down the outside of the core and up through the fuel. If it stops, the core cools itself by conduction and radiation.

- Type: Electric, magnetic bearings
- Flow: ≈ 10 kg/s
- Power draw: ≈ 300 kW

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#ht_circulator

### Helium-to-salt heat exchanger

Hot helium hands its heat to a molten salt here. The salt then leaves the reactor building, so no nuclear system runs through the power plant next door.

- Hot side: Helium, 630 °C in
- Cold side: Nitrate salt, 560 °C out
- Type: Printed-circuit or shell-and-tube

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#ht_ihx

### Molten-salt storage tanks

Two tanks store hot and cold salt. The reactor runs flat out all day. The salt releases heat to the turbine when the data center needs it, like a thermal battery.

- Salt: Sodium and potassium nitrate
- Hot tank: ≈ 560 °C
- Storage: ≈ 8 hours at full output
- Tank size: ≈ 4.5 m dia × 8 m

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#ht_salt

### Steam turbine-generator

Hot salt boils water in a steam generator, and the steam drives this turbine. It is ordinary power-plant equipment, and it can run faster or slower than the reactor because the tanks sit in between.

- Cycle: Steam Rankine
- Electric output: ≈ 5 MWe
- Steam: ≈ 540 °C
- Cooling: Dry air-cooled condenser

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#ht_turbine

## Molten-salt microreactor: how it works

Page: https://microreactors.org/guide/molten-salt-microreactor/

The molten-salt reactor in the park dissolves its fuel in the coolant. If power fails, a frozen plug melts and the fuel drains by gravity into a tank where it cannot stay critical.

### Molten-salt reactor vessel

In this plant the fuel is dissolved in the coolant. A hot salt with uranium in it flows through channels in a graphite block, where it goes critical, and then out to a heat exchanger.

- Fuel salt: Fluoride salt with uranium
- Temperature: ≈ 650 °C at near atmospheric pressure
- Thermal power: ≈ 30 MWt
- Moderator: Graphite

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#ms_vessel

### Fuel-salt pump

A pump on the vessel head moves the fuel salt around the loop. The motor sits above the salt, out of the heat, with a long shaft down to the impeller.

- Type: Vertical shaft, sump pump
- Flow: ≈ 0.5 m³/s
- Shaft seal: Inert gas

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#ms_pump

### Primary heat exchanger

Fuel salt on one side, a clean coolant salt on the other. Fission products stay in the primary loop. The coolant salt carries the heat to the steam plant.

- Type: Shell-and-tube
- Material: Nickel alloy
- Secondary salt: FLiBe or FLiNaK

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#ms_hx

### Freeze plug and drain tank

A small blower keeps a plug of salt frozen in the drain line. If power fails, the blower stops, the plug melts, and the fuel drains by gravity into this tank, where it cannot stay critical and cools passively.

- Plug: Frozen salt, ≈ 20 mm pipe
- Drain time: Minutes
- Tank: Flat, subcritical shape with cooling fins

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#ms_drain

### Off-gas system

Gaseous fission products bubble out of the liquid fuel. The off-gas system pulls them into charcoal beds, holds them while they decay, and keeps the loop clean.

- Gases: Xenon, krypton, tritium
- Hold-up: Charcoal beds, days to weeks
- Carrier: Helium sweep gas

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#ms_offgas

### Steam plant

Coolant salt boils water in the steam generator, and the steam turns the turbine-generator under the canopy. The reactor cell wall sits between here and the fuel.

- Electric output: ≈ 10 MWe
- Steam: ≈ 550 °C
- Cooling: Dry air-cooled condenser

In 3D: https://microreactors.org/#ms_turbine
